rubric: PYTHON AS A FIRST LANGUAGE / BASICS / CHAPTER 3

slides.title: Conditions
slides.main: From logic's “if, then” to executable code: the program starts making decisions.

items.title: Fork
items.sub: The program picks the road itself

items.title: Comparisons
items.sub: Two equals signs ask, one assigns

items.title: Chains
items.sub: From specific to general, top to bottom

body.text: Password check, age discount, overload alarm: real programs make decisions constantly.

slides.title: If and indentation
slides.sub: Condition, colon, and a four-space block
slides.main: Indentation in Python is syntax, not looks: it shows what belongs to the condition.

cells.title: indented
cells.sub: Runs only if the condition is true

cells.title: not indented
cells.sub: Always runs, whatever the check says

slides.title: Comparisons
slides.sub: A comparison gives True or False
slides.main: One equals sign is a command, two are a question.

body.text: `age = 18` is assignment: put a value into a variable; `age == 18` is a comparison.

slides.title: Else: else
slides.sub: What to do when the condition is false
slides.main: Exactly one of the two roads runs: you can rely on that.

cells.title: true →
cells.sub: Upper block: let the user in

cells.title: false →
cells.sub: Lower block: error and a hint

slides.title: Else if: elif
slides.sub: A chain of checks, top to bottom
slides.main: The first matching check runs; the rest are not even considered.

body.text: Order of conditions is program logic: specific to general. General case first, and the specific ones never get a turn.

slides.title: And, or, not
slides.main: “And”: both, “or”: at least one, “not”: flip. De Morgan's laws, now in code.

cells.title: and
cells.sub: True when both parts are true

cells.title: or
cells.sub: True when at least one is true

slides.title: Chained comparisons
slides.main: 0 ≤ x ≤ 100 fits on one line and reads better than two checks.

body.text: Use it for age within limits, server load, a grade on a scale of one to five.

slides.title: Nested conditions
slides.main: A three-floor nesting doll is a signal to simplify: usually a chain or an “and” does it.

cells.title: 3 floors
cells.sub: Hard to see where each block ends

cells.title: 1 floor
cells.sub: An elif chain or one condition with and

slides.title: Comparing strings
slides.main: “yes” and “Yes” are different strings; the in operator checks membership.

body.text:
if answer == "yes":        # "Yes" is already a different string
    print("accepted")

if "error" in message:   # is the word inside the phrase
    print("check the log")
User input is normalized to one case before comparing: otherwise “yes”, “Yes” and “YES” are three answers.

slides.title: Flags and state
slides.sub: A comparison result can be saved
slides.main: A flag is a switch: compare once, pass it on, check later.

cells.title: adult
cells.sub: True or False, with no if at all

cells.title: Program state
cells.sub: Is the user logged in, is the order paid, is the form sent

slides.title: Typical mistakes
slides.main: A number and a string are never equal: “18” and 18 look the same but are different types.

cards.title: age = 18
cards.sub: One sign: assignment instead of a question

cards.title: lost indentation
cards.sub: The block ended sooner than you thought
A number and a string are never equal

cards.title: int(input())
cards.sub: Convert the string to a number first, then compare

body.text: Python does not guess intent: check types, indentation, and equals signs.

slides.title: Reading someone else's code
slides.sub: A chain that gives a grade
slides.main: Say each branch out loud: reading conditions aloud catches half the bugs.

body.text: Only those who scored under 90 reach elif, so no need for “and below 90”: the position in the chain guarantees the bound.
